messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
Marianne had grown up in a small Midwestern town in a house where a caregiver’s anger could arrive without warning and with it came blows she was too young to understand and too frightened to name. As a child she learned to listen for the smallest shifts in a room, for the tone of footsteps, for the sounds that meant someone was near and about to turn on her. She carried that vigilance into adulthood in ways that later seemed, to her, less like habits than conditions for getting through the day. She went on to build a life that looked steady from the outside: she worked for decades as a forester, took pride in knowing the woods, and eventually divorced after a marriage that had never fully reached her. Yet even in the open spaces of her work she found herself arranging her life around danger as she understood it.

In her seventies, Marianne still rises early and goes out to the land she knows best, but she has become careful about who is with her. Being alone with women has become especially unsettling. She cannot explain it in tidy terms, only that a woman’s presence can make her body go rigid and her mind begin searching for what might come next. At work, this has meant finding reasons to leave a break room if a female colleague sits down beside her, or steering conversations toward logistics so she does not have to stay seated across from one woman in a quiet office. Even family gatherings have changed shape for her; if there is only one woman left in the kitchen with her, she will often step outside or offer to fetch something from the truck. She tells herself she is being practical, but the deeper truth is that she is trying to avoid the feeling that another person, especially a woman, might suddenly turn into the kind of threat she knew as a child.

Sounds have also remained charged for her in a way that is hard for others to grasp. Certain related sounds can catch her off guard and bring back the atmosphere of childhood so vividly that she feels briefly removed from the present. The scrape of a chair in an otherwise quiet room, a thud from another part of the house, a sharp sound that resembles movement in a hallway, can make her chest tighten and her attention narrow. What unsettles her even more is silence that comes too abruptly or becomes complete. In a building at work, when the machinery shuts down and the forest office falls suddenly still, she notices it immediately and feels exposed, as though something is about to happen in the gap. In those moments she listens harder, scanning the quiet as if it were a warning sign rather than an absence. She has become known for keeping radios or a television on low in her apartment, not because she wants company, but because she cannot tolerate the dead hush of a room that seems to be holding its breath.

Over the years Marianne also began avoiding exercise, though she does not talk about it as a phobia or a symptom. She simply says she does not see the point, and she has found more ways than one to stay still. Walking for the sake of walking, stretching, anything that makes her body more noticeable to herself, leaves her uneasy. She would rather remain occupied with tasks at the desk or with small chores that keep her hands busy and her attention outward. In the same period she developed another pattern that she describes with embarrassment: she spends money impulsively to distract or comfort herself. After a difficult morning she may buy things she does not need, stopping at stores on the way home from the forest or ordering items online late at night. The purchases give her a brief sense of relief, a few minutes in which she can think about something concrete instead of the familiar surge of fear and shame, though afterward she is left with bills and regret.

Marianne’s life has also become organized around not being alone in a room or building. If she is in her apartment and the neighbors are gone, she feels the walls closing in on her. If she has to lock up the forestry office or be the last person left at a meeting, she hurries, checking the exits and trying not to dwell on the emptiness around her. She will sometimes wait in her car rather than sit by herself inside, even when the weather is poor. Over time these choices have narrowed her world and made her more isolated, though she speaks of them as if they were simple common sense. At the center of it all is a belief she has come to hold with grim certainty: that her life was destroyed by what happened to her, that you can never really know who will harm you, and that in the end she feels more like an object than a person, something acted upon rather than someone with a life of her own.

She sought help after a stretch in which the reminders seemed to be crowding closer together and she could no longer dismiss them as just part of getting older. She was tired of arranging her days around empty rooms, unwanted silences, and the presence of women she could not trust herself to be near. What brought her in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of years spent bracing for harm, spending to soothe herself, and shrinking her life to avoid situations that left her feeling trapped. At intake, Marianne said she did not know whether therapy could give her back anything of what was taken, but she hoped, almost against expectation, that it might help her feel less like an object moving through other people’s spaces and more like a person who still belongs to herself.
